doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Why every vibraphonist sounds different: touch, mallets, Hampton and Norvo
summary: Appleyard explains that touch and mallets give each player a personal sound, and mentions Hampton, Norvo, Tjader and hearing loss.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Before we run out of time I wanted to ask you a question I’ve been thinking about regarding the vibes. If I went to a set of vibes and pushed down the pedal and hit a note with the mallet, and then you went to the vibes and hit it, would it sound that much different?

It’s like with the touch of a pianist. You can have Oscar Peterson sit at a Steinway and play a little bit, and then you’d have Dick Hyman do it, or Teddy Wilson or Billy Charlap, it’d all sound different. It’s the touch. And it’s the same with the mallet. Hampton used to play very softly but with very hard mallets. I use sort of a medium mallet, and at times I can be a little aggressive, because the music inspires you, you

know. I don’t like to play too hard because then there’s a limit as to how much volume you can get. But Hampton and I did a television show together. I had a television series I was the host of, and he came as a guest. And he played first of all, then we got together and we did “Seven Come Eleven” together. And I gave him my instrument and I had another instrument. He picked up my mallets. He started to play. That’s Lionel Hampton. You could hear it right away. Red Norvo was another one. Red Norvo played so beautifully, very low with the mallets. He never looked at the keyboard. He could play like this. I used to impersonate these guys and I laughed and I said I used to wonder what he was looking for, and I think it was looking for a chick you know. Maybe tonight. Cal Tjader was another one that inspired me, told me I should go to New York, it was Cal. And he had a lovely sound. Johnny Ray, this other vibraphone player with Shearing, and Emil did. They all had their own particular sound. And it always amazed me that it varied. And it was the same with pianists. You know I could play a run, and Oscar could be right beside me and it would sound completely different. But it’s the weight, the pressure I guess, and what he hears.

Well that’s a good answer, because you know you would think that well a wind instrument, it might be easier to get your own identifiable sound on a wind instrument I guess, there’s more things that you can vary. But to your ears, the same is for the vibes.

I can pretty well tell the type of instrument that they’re playing. Through the years I’ve become so accustomed to that particular timbre of that instrument. Unfortunately I’m suffering with a hearing loss like we all do. Red could barely hear. You had to yell at him. Hamp too was suffering. But practicing the vibes every day, which I’ve done all my life, you’re exposing yourself to this sound. My specialist told me that if you use an electric toothbrush every day it deteriorates the hearing.
